candidate.answerReason: On the specified interval, the minimum value is 0 and the maximum is 2. Their sum is 2, agreeing with choice B.

methods.label: Split where the absolute values change sign
methods.explanation:
An absolute-value expression changes its algebraic form where its inside expression is zero. Here those points are \(2\), \(3\), and \(4\). Splitting the given interval at these points gives
\[
f(x)=
\begin{cases}
2x-4,&2\le x\le3,\\
8-2x,&3<x<4,\\
0,&4\le x\le8.
\end{cases}
\]
For example, on \([2,3]\), the three absolute values are \(x-2\), \(4-x\), and \(6-2x\), so their stated combination is \(2x-4\). On \((3,4)\), the last absolute value becomes \(2x-6\), giving \(8-2x\). For \(x\ge4\), all three inside expressions are nonnegative and the terms cancel.

The first branch increases from \(0\) at \(x=2\) to \(2\) at \(x=3\). The middle branch stays strictly between \(0\) and \(2\), and the last branch equals \(0\), including both \(x=4\) and \(x=8\). Thus the smallest value is \(0\) and the largest is \(2\). Their sum is \(\boxed{2}\), choice \(\mathrm{B}\).
methods.levelReason: Absolute-value sign cases reduce the problem to increasing, decreasing, and constant linear expressions.

methods.label: Interpret the terms as distances
methods.explanation:
The quantities \(|x-2|\) and \(|x-4|\) are distances from \(x\) to the endpoints \(2\) and \(4\). Also, \(|2x-6|=2|x-3|\) is twice the distance to their midpoint \(3\).

When \(2\le x\le4\), the two endpoint distances add to the segment length \(4-2=2\). Therefore
\[
f(x)=2-2|x-3|.
\]
On this interval, \(0\le|x-3|\le1\), so \(0\le f(x)\le2\). The upper bound is attained at \(x=3\), and the lower bound is attained at \(x=2\) and \(x=4\).

When \(4\le x\le8\), the distance to \(2\) is \((x-3)+1\), while the distance to \(4\) is \((x-3)-1\). Their sum is \(2(x-3)\), exactly twice the distance to \(3\), so \(f(x)=0\).

These two intervals cover the entire domain. Hence the largest value is \(2\), the smallest is \(0\), and their sum is \(\boxed{2}\), choice \(\mathrm{B}\).
methods.levelReason: This uses number-line distances, midpoint relations, and elementary bounds, providing a geometric alternative to sign cases.
